items.prompt: Which top-down structure correctly memoizes solve(state)?
constraints: base(state) can be checked without recursion.

options.text: Compute and return the result, then write it to the cache on the next line.
Check the base; return cache[state] if present; otherwise compute the full result, store it under state, and return it.
Store 0 under state before computing children, then return that cached 0 if state is encountered again.

feedback.reason: A memo entry must map the complete state to its final deterministic result, with lookup before repeated recursion and storage before return.

blocks.text: Base states can return directly or be cached consistently, but nonterminal states need a cache check before expanding dependencies. On a miss, the recurrence is evaluated exactly once, its final value is stored, and all later visits reuse it. Writing a normal answer before computation can corrupt acyclic logic and does not solve cycles. Memoization is an implementation of a proven state and transition, not a substitute for them.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.store_placeholder: A placeholder is not the solved value and can be mistaken for a legitimate result. Cycles require an explicit in-progress policy, not an ordinary answer entry.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.cache_after_return: Code after return is unreachable, so repeated states are never stored and recomputation remains.

items.prompt: A recurrence solve(i, j) compares suffixes of two strings. Which memo key is correct?
constraints: i and j can change independently.
The result is deterministic for each suffix pair.

options.text: Use the pair (i, j).
Use only i because it is the first argument.
Use recursion depth because calls at the same depth have consumed the same total number of characters.

feedback.reason: The cache identity must match the semantic state identity, which here is the full pair (i, j).

blocks.text: Memoization replaces repeated evaluation with table lookup, so a key collision is equivalent to declaring two states equal. Since either string can advance independently, one i corresponds to multiple unresolved second-string suffixes. Recursion depth also loses how progress is distributed between the strings. Use a canonical representation of all state components and no irrelevant history.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.i_key: Different j values pair the same first-string suffix with different second-string suffixes, so they can have different answers.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.depth_key: The same depth can contain different (i, j) splits and therefore different suffix pairs.

items.prompt: A conceptual R by C state space exists, but obstacles make only K states reachable from the start. Each reached state has O(1) outgoing transitions. Select the memoized time and cache space.
constraints: Cache operations are O(1) expected time.
The recursion never evaluates unreachable states.

feedback.reason: Memoization evaluates and stores each reachable state once, so its principal cost follows K rather than the full rectangle.

blocks.text: Each of the K reachable states is expanded once and performs constant transition work, giving O(K) time. The memo table holds O(K) values; the call stack may add up to path depth, which is at most O(K), so O(K) remains a valid total bound. When K is close to R·C, tabulation may perform the same asymptotic work with lower recursion overhead. Memoization is conditionally advantageous, not universally faster.

items.prompt: Order the checks for a safe memoized recursion.
constraints: The intended DP recurrence should terminate without fixed-point iteration.
A state may have multiple dependencies.

elements.text: Identify a measure that strictly progresses toward a terminal state on every recursive edge.
Define terminal states for that measure.
Check whether the complete state already has a finished cached result.
Recursively compute missing dependencies, then store the finished result.

feedback.reason: Termination and dependency direction must be established before a cache can safely reuse completed results.

blocks.text: Prove termination before wrapping the recurrence in a cache

items: Identify a well-founded measure that strictly moves toward termination on every recursive dependency.
Define the terminal states reached when that measure reaches its boundary.
For a nonterminal call, return an existing finished result keyed by the complete state.
On a miss, compute all terminating dependencies, store the finished result, and then return it.

blocks.text: A cache prevents repeated expansion of finished states; it does not make an unfinished cycle terminate. If a dependency can revisit the same in-progress state, the problem needs an explicit cycle or fixed-point contract rather than an ordinary answer entry.

blocks.title: Memoization order
blocks.text: Progress proof → terminal bases → finished-result lookup → compute, store and return.

items.prompt: A memoized solver stores only states it reaches. Does that fact alone justify deleting older cache entries during the same recursion while preserving the memoized time bound and any reconstruction contract?
constraints: Future recursive branches may reach states in a nonlocal order.
No liveness proof has been made.

options.text: Yes. Any memo table is automatically a state-compressed DP.
Yes. A state can always be deleted immediately after its current caller returns.
No. Sparse allocation and safe eviction are different properties; a later branch may still request an older state.

feedback.reason: Memoization is demand-driven storage, but eviction requires a separate proof that the value is dead for all remaining computation.

blocks.text: A sparse cache can be much smaller than a full rectangular table when few states are reached. That does not imply a simple chronological retention window because recursive traversal can return and later enter a different branch that converges on an earlier state. Deleting the entry would preserve correctness only if it is recomputed, but can destroy the intended complexity benefit; in some formulations it can also break reconstruction. Compression must follow dependency liveness, not the fact that storage is a map.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_sparse: Memoization avoids allocating unreachable states, but retained reached states may remain reusable throughout the traversal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_after_return: Another branch higher in the recursion can later converge on the same state, which is precisely the reuse memoization was meant to preserve.

items.prompt: A state can legitimately have 0 valid completions. Which cache check is correct?
constraints: The cache supports an explicit membership operation.

options.text: Store only nonzero results because zero cannot help another branch.
If cache contains state, return cache[state], even when the stored value is 0.
If cache[state] is truthy, return it; otherwise recompute.

feedback.reason: Presence and value are separate facts; zero is a valid cached result, not a cache miss.

blocks.text: A memo table represents a partial mapping from state to solved result. The mapping can contain any value allowed by the recurrence, including zero. Testing truthiness conflates the domain value with membership and can restore exponential recomputation over impossible regions. Use an explicit sentinel outside the value domain or a membership operation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.truthy: A cached zero is a finished answer, but a truthiness check misclassifies it as missing and repeats work.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.nonzero_only: Repeated impossible states can be common; caching zero prevents their subtrees from being explored again.

items.prompt: A path solver uses solve(r, c) and returns 0 outside the grid, 1 at the destination, otherwise the sum of down and right calls. Which memoization plan preserves the recurrence?
constraints: Only in-grid nonterminal states need ordinary cache entries.
Different paths can reach the same cell.

options.text: Use (r, c) as the key; handle out-of-grid and destination bases; on a miss compute both successors, store their sum, and return it.
Use r as the key because all cells in a row have the same distance to the bottom.
Cache the result of only the down branch and recompute the right branch every time.

feedback.reason: The cache key and stored value must correspond exactly to the full cell state and its complete transition result.

blocks.text: The destination and out-of-grid checks establish terminal values. For any other cell, the state result is the sum of both legal successor counts, so that full sum is what belongs under key (r, c). Multiple incoming paths can then reuse the exact cell result. Partial branch caching or row-only keys fail because they no longer map a complete state to its defined answer.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.row_cache: Column changes the remaining grid region and path count, so row-only entries alias distinct subproblems.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.cache_branch: The cached value would not represent solve(r, c), so returning it as the state result would violate the state contract and leave overlap unhandled.

items.prompt: A memoized function solve(i, budget, mode) can take different transitions for different mode values. Which cache design is sound?

options.text: Key by the complete future-relevant state tuple (i, budget, mode).
Key only by i because memoization merges all calls at one position.
Key only by budget because mode affects transitions but not the input suffix.
Keep one global result because recursive calls eventually return to the same root.

feedback.reason: Memoization is valid only when equal keys imply equal future subproblems and answers.

blocks.text: If budget or mode changes which branches are legal or valuable, calls that share only i are not equivalent. The key must encode every dimension that can affect the remaining recurrence. Extra irrelevant history may be omitted, but future-relevant state cannot.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.index_only: Different budgets or modes at one index can produce different answers.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.budget_only: The remaining suffix and mode still affect future choices.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.last_result: A recursive tree contains many distinct subproblems, not one answer per root invocation.

items.prompt: A proposed recurrence can call solve(i) again without changing i on one branch. What must be checked before claiming ordinary memoization gives a terminating DP?

options.text: Prove progress toward a base state or define cycle handling; caching a state only after it returns does not break a recursive cycle.
Memoization guarantees termination because every call has a key.
Delete the key whenever a state is entered so recursion can continue freely.
Ignore self-calls because the eventual cached result will overwrite them.

feedback.reason: Memoization removes repeated completed work but does not by itself resolve a recursive dependency cycle.

blocks.text: A well-founded DP state decreases a measure or reaches a declared base. If a call re-enters the same unresolved state before its first computation finishes, a simple cache lookup may miss and recurse forever. The recurrence needs a progress proof or explicit cycle semantics such as visitation states.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.memo_always_terminates: A cache does not contain a value for a state whose first evaluation is still in progress.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.delete_key_on_entry: Deleting keys removes reuse and does not provide a cycle result.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_self_call: An unresolved self-dependency cannot be replaced by a later cache write without a defined fixed-point rule.

items.prompt: Which ordering of operations is required in a top-down memoized recurrence?

elements.text: Handle the base case for the current state.
Return a stored result if the state is already cached.
Compute the transition branches and aggregate their results.
Store the computed result under the complete state key.

feedback.reason: Base and cache checks avoid unnecessary work; only a miss reaches the transition, whose result is stored under the state just solved.

blocks.text: A base result can be returned immediately. For non-base states, a valid cached result must be recognized even when its value is zero or negative, so presence is separate from truthiness. Only a miss computes branches and then records the answer for future calls.

items.prompt: What is the canonical order for a top-down memoized helper?

options.text: Handle the base case, return a cached result if present, otherwise compute children and store the result.
Always recurse into children before checking the cache.
Store the raw input and never store the subproblem result.
Cache only the root answer after all recursion finishes.

feedback.reason: Checking the cache before branching is what prevents recomputation of a solved state.

blocks.text: Base cases may precede the cache or be included in the cache contract. The essential invariant is that a computed state is stored before callers reuse it.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.branch-before-cache: It recomputes the same descendants before discovering a cached answer.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.store-input: Memoization caches outputs by state, not only raw input.

items.prompt: What is the main correctness requirement for a memo table key?

options.text: It includes every state component that can change the subproblem result.
The first index is always enough, even with capacity or alignment context.
It records only the order in which the state was reached.
Any short hash is correct even if different states collide.

feedback.reason: Different result-determining states must not share a cache entry.

blocks.text: For a sequence alignment or capacity problem, the key may require two indices or an index-plus-budget. Hashing can encode the key, but collisions must not merge semantic states.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.index-only: Omitted constraints produce wrong cache reuse.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.call-order: Reach history is not necessarily the subproblem identity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.random-hash: A lossy key can return the wrong state's result.

items.prompt: When can top-down memoization use less time than filling a complete bottom-up table?

options.text: When only a sparse subset of theoretically possible states is reachable from the original query.
When every possible state is required and no transition is computed.
When repeated states are never cached.
When states are sorted before recursion.

feedback.reason: Top-down evaluates demand-reachable states while bottom-up may materialize the full rectangular domain.

blocks.text: Both methods can have the same worst-case state count. The advantage depends on reachability, transition cost, and cache overhead.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all-states-needed: If every state is needed, top-down has little sparsity benefit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no-cache: Without caching, repeated subproblems can make top-down worse.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort-table: Sorting is not the source of sparse-state savings.

items.prompt: What must distinguish an uncomputed memo entry from a valid computed result of zero?

options.text: Use a separate uncomputed marker or a presence flag rather than zero itself.
Use zero for both because recomputing zero is harmless to correctness and cost.
Use -1 even when valid results can be -1.
Avoid caching any state that might return zero.

feedback.reason: Zero can be a legitimate DP result, so it cannot always mean absent from the cache.

blocks.text: A separate boolean, optional value, or impossible sentinel preserves both correctness and memoization of zero-valued states.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero-uncomputed: Repeated recomputation can be exponential and can also confuse cache semantics.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.negative-only: A sentinel must be outside the valid result domain.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no-cache: Valid zero results should still be reusable.
